conflicts/albigensian-crusade/name: The Albigensian Crusade against the Cathars
conflicts/albigensian-crusade/religionRo: This was the first crusade proclaimed by a pope against heretics inside Latin Christendom, with the full crusade indulgence offered for forty days’ service; the stated and real aim was the destruction of the Cathar ‘good men’ and the punishment of lords who protected them. Land, lordship and the expansion of the Capetian monarchy into the south quickly became major motives, especially for Simon de Montfort and later Louis VIII. Historians also debate the target itself: Malcolm Barber and Bernard Hamilton see an organised dualist church with Balkan links, while R. I. Moore and Mark Pegg argue that ‘Catharism’ as a unified counter-church was partly constructed by its persecutors.

conflicts/albigensian-crusade/summary: Proclaimed by Innocent III after the murder of his legate in 1208, the Albigensian Crusade sent northern French armies into Languedoc to destroy Catharism and the lords who sheltered it. It began with the massacre at Béziers in 1209, saw mass burnings of Cathars at Minerve, Lavaur and elsewhere, and became a war of conquest led by Simon de Montfort and finally by the French crown. The Treaty of Paris in 1229 brought Toulouse under Capetian control, and the Inquisition followed.
conflicts/albigensian-crusade/story:
By the late twelfth century Languedoc, a land of cities and of independent-minded nobility under the counts of Toulouse and the Trencavel viscounts, was home to many followers of the ‘good men’ (bons homes), whom Catholic writers called Cathars or Albigensians. They taught a dualist faith in which the material world was the work of an evil principle, and they offered salvation through the consolamentum received from ascetic perfected believers. Missions by Bernard of Clairvaux in 1145, the Third Lateran Council’s condemnation of 1179 and preaching by Cistercians and, from 1206, by Bishop Diego of Osma and Dominic of Caleruega, who debated Cathars at Montréal and Fanjeaux, had little success.

In January 1208 the papal legate Pierre de Castelnau was murdered near Saint-Gilles after excommunicating Count Raymond VI of Toulouse; Innocent III blamed the count and in March called the nobility of northern France to a crusade, granting the same indulgence as for the Holy Land in return for forty days’ service. Raymond VI submitted to public penance at Saint-Gilles in June 1209 and joined the crusade himself, which turned the army against his nephew Raymond-Roger Trencavel. On 22 July 1209 the crusaders stormed Béziers. The inhabitants, Catholics as well as Cathars, were massacred, including those who had fled into the church of the Madeleine; the legate Arnaud Amalric reported to the pope that ‘nearly twenty thousand’ were killed, a figure historians regard as exaggerated. The saying ‘Kill them all; God will know his own’, attributed to him by Caesarius of Heisterbach some years later, is of doubtful authenticity but reflects how the event was remembered.

Carcassonne surrendered on 15 August 1209; Raymond-Roger Trencavel was imprisoned and died there in November, and Simon de Montfort, a veteran of the Fourth Crusade who had refused to attack Zara, was given his lands. Montfort waged a relentless war of sieges. At Minerve in 1210 about 140 Cathar perfecti who refused to recant were burned; at Lavaur in 1211 the lord Aimery of Montréal and some eighty knights were hanged or put to the sword, the lady Guiraude was thrown into a well and stoned, and around three hundred or more heretics were burned. Southern forces also killed crusaders and mutilated prisoners, and Montfort answered with mutilations of his own, as at Bram in 1210, where captives had their eyes put out and noses cut off.

The war widened when Peter II of Aragon, overlord of many southern lords and victor over the Almohads at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212, came to defend his vassals. On 12 September 1213 Montfort’s much smaller army defeated and killed him at Muret. The Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 confirmed Montfort as count of Toulouse, but the south rose again: Raymond VII retook Beaucaire in 1216, Toulouse rebelled in 1217, and on 25 June 1218 Simon de Montfort was killed by a stone from a siege engine, operated by the city’s women according to the Song of the Cathar Wars. In 1219 the future Louis VIII took part in the massacre of the population of Marmande.

Amaury de Montfort could not hold his father’s conquests and in 1224 ceded his rights to the French crown. Louis VIII led a royal crusade in 1226, took Avignon after a siege and received the submission of much of the south before dying of dysentery that November. The regent Blanche of Castile pursued the war until Raymond VII accepted the Treaty of Meaux-Paris in April 1229, doing public penance at Notre-Dame, agreeing to pursue heretics, endow a university at Toulouse and marry his heiress to a brother of the king, which brought the county to the crown in 1271.

The Council of Toulouse in 1229 organised the hunt for heretics, and from 1233–1234 Gregory IX entrusted inquisitions to the Dominicans. After the killing of inquisitors at Avignonet in 1242, a royal army besieged the mountain refuge of Montségur; when it surrendered in March 1244 more than two hundred Cathars who refused to recant were burned. Quéribus fell in 1255, and the last known Cathar perfect in Languedoc, Guilhem Bélibaste, was burned in 1321. The independence of the southern principalities and much of the courtly culture of the troubadours did not survive.
conflicts/albigensian-crusade/nameOfGod: Innocent III presented the crusade as a war of the Church against heretics more dangerous than Saracens, offering the Holy Land indulgence for forty days’ service. Crusaders wore the cross, and Cistercian legates such as Arnaud Amalric directed the campaigns; the chronicler Peter of les Vaux-de-Cernay praised the burnings as acts of faith, writing that the crusaders burned heretics ‘with great joy’. Montfort’s victory at Muret was hailed as a miracle and divine verdict, and the crusade was described as the ‘business of peace and faith’ (negotium pacis et fidei).
conflicts/albigensian-crusade/religiousC: The spread of Catharism and of Waldensian preaching in Languedoc, which the papacy saw as a threat to the salvation of souls and to the unity of the Church.
Innocent III’s conviction that secular lords who tolerated heresy forfeited their right to rule, so that their lands could be ‘exposed to seizure’ by Catholics.
The failure of preaching missions by Cistercians, Diego of Osma and Dominic to win the region back.
The murder of the papal legate Pierre de Castelnau in January 1208, which Innocent treated as martyrdom and an assault on the Church.
conflicts/albigensian-crusade/otherCause: The ambitions of northern French nobles, above all Simon de Montfort, to win lands and titles in the rich south.
The Capetian monarchy’s long-term interest in extending royal power to the Mediterranean, achieved by 1229–1271.
The weakness and fragmentation of authority in Languedoc and the rivalry between the counts of Toulouse, the Trencavels and the crown of Aragon.
Cultural and linguistic differences between the Occitan south and the French-speaking north, which sharpened hostility on both sides.

conflicts/albigensian-crusade/triggers/2: The fall of Béziers on 22 July 1209, which terrified the south into surrender and set the pattern of the war.

conflicts/albigensian-crusade/keyPeople/: Proclaimed the crusade in 1208 and set its legal and spiritual terms.
Tried at times to restrain Montfort’s land-grabbing but confirmed his conquests at the Fourth Lateran Council.
Abbot of Cîteaux and papal legate
Led the crusade army in 1209 and reported the massacre at Béziers as a divine judgement.
Became archbishop of Narbonne in 1212 and later quarrelled with Montfort over the duchy of Narbonne.
Conquered most of Languedoc through sieges, burnings and the victory at Muret.
Killed at the siege of Toulouse in 1218; his son Simon became the English baronial leader.
Accused of protecting heretics and of the legate’s murder; switched sides and finally led southern resistance.
Died excommunicate in 1222 and was refused Christian burial.
Led the reconquest of the south after 1216 and resisted Louis VIII.
Accepted the Treaty of Paris in 1229; his lands passed to the crown in 1271.
Seized during negotiations and died in his own prison in November 1209.
King of Aragon, overlord in Languedoc
A Catholic king crowned by Innocent III, he intervened to protect his southern vassals from Montfort.
Killed at Muret in 1213, ending Aragonese ambitions north of the Pyrenees.
Preacher and founder of the Order of Preachers
Preached and debated with Cathars from 1206 and founded a house for converted women at Prouille; he accompanied the crusading period, though his part in its violence is debated.
His order, approved in 1216, later supplied the inquisitors of Languedoc.
conflicts/albigensian-crusade/casualties: No reliable total exists. Contemporary figures are rhetorical: Arnaud Amalric claimed nearly 20,000 killed at Béziers and the Song of the Cathar Wars claimed 5,000 at Marmande, numbers historians consider inflated. Chroniclers give more credible counts for specific burnings (about 140 at Minerve, around 300–400 at Lavaur, more than 200 at Montségur). Popular claims of hundreds of thousands or a million dead have no scholarly basis; the total probably ran into tens of thousands over twenty years, but this cannot be established.
conflicts/albigensian-crusade/effects/0: The independent principalities of Languedoc were destroyed and the region was absorbed into the kingdom of France, which gained a Mediterranean coast.
conflicts/albigensian-crusade/effects/1: Many southern noble families were dispossessed, creating a class of exiles (faidits) who sheltered heretics and resisted for decades.
conflicts/albigensian-crusade/effects/2: The Occitan troubadour culture declined, though its poetry preserved bitter protests against the crusade and Rome.
conflicts/albigensian-crusade/effects/3: The Crown of Aragon turned its expansion south and into the Mediterranean after the defeat at Muret.
conflicts/albigensian-crusade/effectsOnC: It established that crusade, with its indulgence, could be used against heretics and Christian lords within Christendom, a precedent used against the Hohenstaufen, the Hussites and others.

It led directly to the papal Inquisition: the Council of Toulouse (1229) and Gregory IX’s commissions to Dominican inquisitors from 1233–1234 created lasting procedures of investigation, penance and burning.
Catharism was largely eradicated in Languedoc by the early fourteenth century, after decades of inquisition rather than the war alone.
The Dominican Order, born in this mission field, grew into a major preaching and teaching order, though its association with the Inquisition shaped its later image.
conflicts/albigensian-crusade/legacy: The Albigensian Crusade remains one of the most contested episodes in church history: a byword for religious violence (‘Kill them all…’), a source of Occitan regional identity, and a subject of romantic modern myths about Cathar treasure and Gnostic wisdom. Historians continue to debate how far Catharism was a coherent church and how far the crusade was driven by faith or by conquest, but agree that it turned crusading inward and launched the systematic inquisition of heresy.
conflicts/albigensian-crusade/dissenters: Protested to Innocent III in 1213 that the crusade was despoiling Catholic lords who were not heretics; the pope briefly suspended crusade privileges for Languedoc before reversing himself under pressure from his legates.
Anonymous continuator of the Song of the Cathar Wars

A Catholic Occitan poet who wrote the second part of the Song denounced the crusaders’ cruelty and greed and portrayed Simon de Montfort’s death as just retribution, while professing loyalty to the Church.
The Toulousain troubadour’s song ‘D’un sirventes far’ (c. 1228) attacked Rome for preaching crusade against Christians, accusing it of selling pardons and leading the faithful to death.
In 1213 the pope wrote that the business of the faith was being turned to the seizure of lands and ordered restraint, though he did not end the crusade.
conflicts/albigensian-crusade/theatres/0: Saint-Gilles: murder of the legate and penance of Raymond VI
conflicts/albigensian-crusade/theatres/6: Siege of Toulouse: death of Simon de Montfort
conflicts/albigensian-crusade/campaigns/: Northern French crusaders under the legate Arnaud Amalric, joined by Raymond VI
Gathering at Lyon in June 1209, the army marched down the Rhône valley into Languedoc, stormed Béziers on 22 July and forced Carcassonne to surrender on 15 August.
Simon de Montfort’s war of sieges
Simon de Montfort and crusader contingents
From his base at Carcassonne Montfort reduced the fortresses of the Minervois and Corbières, took Lavaur, defeated Peter II at Muret and died besieging rebellious Toulouse.
King Louis VIII and the royal army
The king’s army descended the Rhône, besieged Avignon for three months, received the submission of much of Languedoc, and turned home; Louis died of dysentery at Montpensier in November 1226.
